source.title: Scaling Self-Play with Self-Guidance
source.authors: Luke Bailey; Kaiyue Wen; Kefan Dong; Tatsunori Hashimoto; Tengyu Ma

record.tranche_reason: The study measures compute scaling for self-play theorem-proving solve rates, not the held-out pretraining loss, parameter/token scaling, or compute-optimal allocation in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper fits sigmoidal curves to cumulative solve rate on training problems as a function of model generations. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss, sweep parameter count or training tokens, or find a compute-optimal parameter/token split. Its results below are adjacent self-play scaling findings, not tests of the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study fits sigmoid curves to cumulative solve rate on a fixed set of Lean4 training problems against the number of self-play generations, for one fixed 7B model. It measures no held-out pretraining loss and sweeps no parameters or tokens. It finds no compute-optimal split, varies no architecture, and relates no downstream performance to scale or loss. It borrows the 'scaling law' framing as an evaluation tool for comparing RL and self-play methods, so it tests none of V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that existing self-play plateaus because the Conjecturer collapses and the Solver's entropy collapses. SGS, which adds a Guide and uses the REINFORCE1/2 Solver objective, sustains learning: about 7% higher fitted asymptotic solve rate than RL, and the 7B model surpasses 671B pass@4. Scaling across model size is left to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures cumulative theorem-proving solve rate versus self-play generations and fits a sigmoid; it does not reproduce pretraining loss sweeps over parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: For SGS sigmoid fits, early low-compute points disproportionately influence fitted parameters; the authors omit data below 100,000 generations. The fitted asymptote varies with end-of-run data removal and random 50% subsampling.

fits_no_version.finding: For DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B on D3k, cumulative solve rate versus generations fits a sigmoid in log compute. The fitted asymptote is 67.1% for SGS, 65.5% for No Guide and 60.3% for the REINFORCE1/2 baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In LLM RL/self-play, cumulative solve rate versus compute follows a sigmoid in log compute, whose asymptote can be used to compare methods.

fits_no_version.finding: The SGS fitted asymptote drops from 67.1% to 65.9% when the last 30% of the data is removed, and has a 1.1% standard deviation across 50% random subsamples. The authors also report that early low-compute points distort the fits, so they drop data below 100k generations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sigmoid compute-scaling fits for RL accuracy depend on which data are included in the fit, especially the early low-compute points.

record.problems: The experiments hold model size fixed and use a single formal theorem-proving dataset. The authors note that true asymptotic solve rates are unobservable, and that fitted asymptotes within 1.1% should be treated cautiously. Several comparisons are reported through figures rather than exact text values.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results relevant to the claim were left out. Other reported training dynamics and ablations concern Solver entropy, Conjecturer rewards, and synthetic-problem properties rather than the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss and power-law scaling in parameters, tokens or compute: all untested.
Extrapolation from small pretraining runs to much larger ones: untested. The sigmoid asymptote extrapolation concerns RL solve rate, not loss.
Model shape or architecture at fixed parameter count: untested.
The power-law form in other regimes: untested. The study uses a sigmoid on a bounded accuracy metric in RL/self-play and does not test whether a power law holds.
Downstream performance predicted by scale or pretraining loss: untested. Model size is held fixed.
Sensitivity of pretraining-law exponents or compute-optimal splits to fitting choices: untested. Only the study's own sigmoid fit is checked for sensitivity.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Its use of the phrase 'scaling laws' refers to sigmoidal accuracy-versus-compute fits in the style of Khatri et al. and Ruan et al., not to loss power laws. The reader's T6 classification and all rows marked none are correct. T4 could also be argued, since the authors use scaling-law fitting as a tool, but the fitted law is not the claim's power law.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute is tested.
No power laws fitted on small pretraining runs are used to predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameter count and training tokens is tested.
Depth, width, and architecture are not varied at fixed parameter count.
The study does not test whether the pretraining-loss power-law form holds in another modality or training regime.
The study measures cumulative solve rate on the self-play training set, not downstream task performance predicted by scale or pretraining loss.
It studies sensitivity of sigmoid fits to data selection, but does not test pretraining-loss power-law exponents, compute-optimal splits, or departures from a single power law.
